processing: Orthodox Ceylon black tea in grades such as BOPF and BOPF.Sp, with seasonal lots valued most.
harvest_season: Year-round, with the prized Uva seasonal lots shaped by the dry weather of the region's quality season, usually in the middle of the year.
appearance_dry: Small dark broken leaf in the BOPF grades, the ones this estate is best known for.
appearance_liquor: Bright coppery red, typical of seasonal Uva.
taste_profile: Classic Uva character in the seasonal lots: as with other Uva teas, brisk and penetrating with a cooling, slightly medicinal lift.

brewing.notes: Brewed Western style. These small grades are quick, so start at two and a half minutes. Try seasonal lots without milk first.

vintage_note: Sold through the Colombo auction by grade, and to consumers often as a named seasonal Uva of a stated year, such as Seasonal Uva 2024. Seasonal lots are limited, so the year matters; drink them within a year or two while the aroma holds.
description:
Uva Highlands is an estate at Bandarawela, run by Malwatte Valley Plantations and sitting at about 1,250 metres.

Its reputation rests on seasonal teas. Uva's dry spell can give the leaf a sharp aromatic edge you will not get at other times, and this estate's small BOPF grades have been among the ones that show it at auction.

In the cup, seasonal lots are brisk and bright with a cooling note, typical of good Uva. Small grades extract quickly, so a long steep turns them harsh; keep it short and taste before adding milk.

When buying, ask whether a lot is seasonal and from which year. A non-seasonal tea from the same estate is a good everyday cup, but a different thing.
history:
The estate is said to have been first planted in 1915, a date that rests on trade reports rather than a detailed record.

In recent years it has been known mostly for auction results, including Rs. 1,950 per kilo for a BOPF.Sp in May 2022, bought by Unilever Lipton Ceylon.
